transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-21
Time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Diego (Redwood SE), Liam (AtlasPay Head of ML), Sara (Product Lead), Owen (Infra)

Summary: quick intro then ran through AtlasPay's current stack and constraints. Customer asked about dedicated pools, how bursting to hosted works, what isolation guarantees look like, and what autoscaling patterns Redwood supports. Security/compliance questions about KMS and audit logs. Agreed on next steps: pricing, security docs, and a benchmark run with sample workload.

Transcript:
00:00 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time today, appreciate it. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood team, and Diego who you'll hear from a lot is our SE focused on Dedicated and Private deployments.
00:12 Liam: Hey, thanks Maya. I'm Liam, lead for ML at AtlasPay. We have Sara and Owen on as well.
00:19 Sara: hi all, thanks for setting this up.
00:22 Diego: Great, quick agenda - understand your workload, constraints, latency targets, and then we can map to Dedicated vs Private and discuss burst/fallback. Sound good?
00:31 Owen: yep good. quick context: we process payment-related messages for merchant integrations. Latency target is sub-200ms for 95th p99 we mean p95 ideally under 150ms for small chat-style prompts and up to 800ms for longer batch scoring. 
00:49 Liam: We currently run some open models in-house on spot infra but we're hitting variability and the ops overhead is high. We're evaluating Redwood Dedicated because we want reserved GPUs and predictable throughput — and isolation due to PCI-related concerns.
01:05 Maya: Totally makes sense. Can you give a sense of current concurrency and token rates — peaks and troughs?
01:12 Liam: Baseline is about 20 concurrent requests, peaks around 150 during merchant settlement windows which last maybe 10-15 minutes. Token rate averages ~120k tokens/minute at peak. We're ok with short bursts but need predictable tail latency.
01:29 Diego: That's helpful. For Dedicated we typically size reserved pools by peak QPS/throughput and then configure autoscale/route bursting. Two approaches: 1) keep enough reserved to meet p95 targets and then burst to hosted capacity for overflow; 2) reserve for steady-state and accept slightly higher tail latency during peaks. Which is closer to your tolerance?
01:51 Sara: Option 1 is preferred — we don't want to expose merchants to higher tail latency during settlement windows. But cost matters. Curious about pricing for both reserved and burst-to-hosted.
02:02 Maya: We'll include a couple pricing buckets in the follow-up. To clarify technical behavior: when you burst to hosted, requests are routed to Redwood's hosted fleet seamlessly; sensitive requests can be filtered or we can route only non-PII workloads. Also we have options for encrypted in-transit and at-rest keys — you can bring-your-own KMS.
02:21 Owen: For us isolation means no noisy neighbors and separate NVMe volumes for logs. Also we need to know about network egress controls and whether we can peer — we must avoid routing data through public internet.
02:33 Diego: For Dedicated we support VPC peering and private link; traffic stays within the peered network. We also support dedicated nodes with isolated tenants; logs can be shipped to your S3 or to an on-prem logging endpoint.
02:44 Liam: Good. On compliance: we need SOC2 type II, ability to configure key rotation via our KMS, audit logs, and SSO with SCIM/SAML. How mature are those?
02:55 Maya: We're SOC2 certified, we have documentation and an attestation we can share. KMS integrations are supported — you can use customer-managed keys. SSO/SAML + SCIM are available for team provisioning. We'll send the security pack after this call.
03:08 Owen: Any differences in data retention settings between Hosted and Dedicated? We need log retention to meet 7-year retention for specific audit trails.
03:18 Diego: You can configure retention policies and export raw logs. For Dedicated customers we provide more control over retention. We'll outline retention options in the security doc.
03:27 Sara: On the performance side — what kind of latency numbers can we expect on Dedicated vs Hosted? We want realistic numbers for the model family we plan to run; right now it's a mixture of Llama2-13B-type open weights and a quantized 7B for cheaper invites.
03:44 Diego: Typically Dedicated gives you predictable latency since GPUs are reserved and we tune batching. For Llama2-13B the p95 on A100 class would be X ms for short prompts — note: (recording: could be 60-90ms) — and quantized 7B typically under 30-50ms depending on kernel and KV cache hit rate. Actual numbers depend on sequence lengths and KV cache warming. We'll run a benchmark for your exact prompts.
04:08 Liam: Can you explain KV cache behavior? We have conversational flows where caching prefixes matter a lot.
04:13 Diego: Sure. We support KV cache warmup and prefix caching. If you have long conversation histories, we can keep hot KV cache for pinned sessions. That reduces token cost and latency dramatically. For Dedicated you can control cache eviction policies more tightly.
04:27 Owen: Autoscaling question — how fast can dedicated pools scale? We have 10 minute settlement spikes; we need capacity within that window.
04:36 Diego: Dedicated typically scales with a couple knobs: scheduled scaling (pre-warm GPUs ahead of expected spikes) and reactive scaling for longer-term trends. For sub-10 minute spikes we recommend scheduled pre-warm or using burst-to-hosted where the hosted fleet can absorb immediate spikes. In practice, warming GPUs from cold can take several minutes depending on model and weight transfer.
04:57 Liam: So to meet our <150ms p95 during 10-minute spikes we should probably schedule pre-warm for known windows and use hosted burst for unexpected overflow.
05:06 Maya: That pattern is common. We'll show an example plan in the follow-up: reserved pool sized for baseline + scheduled pre-warms for daily windows, plus a burst-to-hosted policy with a hard cap and SLA for overflow routing.
05:18 Sara: Any option for hybrid where sensitive traffic stays on Dedicated, but less-sensitive inference goes to Hosted?
05:24 Diego: Yes, route-by-policy is exactly that — you can tag requests and route only non-sensitive to hosted, or route based on model variant.
05:30 Owen: How are rollouts handled? We need canary deploys and automatic fallback to previous model on quality regressions.
05:36 Diego: Redwood supports canary and A/B rollouts with traffic split, automatic health checks, and fallback policies. We also integrate with evals to detect regressions on your prompt sets.
05:47 Liam: Great. On cost — give me a ballpark: if we reserve — say — 8 A100-equivalent GPUs, what's the expected committed monthly cost vs bursting?
05:56 Maya: We'll include exact numbers in the deck, but high level: reserved is typically a 30-50% discount vs on-demand hosted. Burst calls are billed at higher on-demand rates; we'll show a blended estimate based on your traffic profile.
06:07 Sara: Competitors we're looking at are SageMaker endpoints and Run:AI; curious about ease-of-integration and observability differences.
06:16 Diego: Compared to SageMaker our selling points are optimized inference runtime, prefix caching, built-in cost controls and per-route dashboards, plus simpler (developer-first) APIs. Run:AI focuses on orchestration; Redwood bundles runtime optimizations with the platform.
06:29 Owen: Any limits on model bring-your-own? We want to run some internally fine-tuned artifacts and custom kernels.
06:35 Diego: You can bring your own models. For Dedicated we handle model installation and compatibility checks; custom kernels are something we'd evaluate — usually okay but we'd run a compatibility test during onboarding.
06:46 Liam: Ok. For the benchmark, what do you need from us?
06:49 Diego: Sample payloads, a representative traffic timeline (typical and peak), and a few prompt sets for quality and latency. Ideally a dockerized inference runner or just model artifacts and a few script inputs. Also any constraints — egress rules, IP allow lists for peering.
07:04 Owen: I'll share our traffic patterns and network constraints.
07:08 Maya: Awesome. Quick product note: Dedicated includes per-token cost breakdowns, per-route latency histograms, and a KV cache hit-rate metric you can track in the console.
07:18 Sara: That visibility will help justify the reserved cost to our finance team.
07:22 Liam: Any concerns around data persistence? We want to ensure model input is not persisted beyond X days.
07:28 Diego: We have data retention controls. For Dedicated customers we can set shorter retention windows or auto-delete logs; plus the ability to export logs to your storage if needed.
07:39 Maya: Ok let's recap next steps and owners?
07:41 Liam: please do.
07:42 Maya: We'll send: 1) pricing and capacity options with 12/36 month reserved tiers and burst pricing, 2) SOC2/security pack and KMS integration guide, 3) a proposed benchmark plan from Diego. Diego will follow up to schedule the run. Owen will send network topology and sample workload.
07:58 Sara: Perfect.
08:00 Liam: Sounds good, thanks everyone.
08:03 Maya: Thanks all. We'll follow up by Friday with the docs and proposed schedule.

(occasional crosstalk and short filler words present in original audio; some transcription noise: names and acronyms may be slightly off in automated transcript)

End of meeting.
